primary_sources.author: Annambhaṭṭa
primary_sources.edition: Ganganatha Jha edition with Dīpikā and Nyāya-Bodhinī commentaries
primary_sources.role: Primary definitional source for all five hetvābhāsa categories and their sub-types

primary_sources.author: Anonymous (pedagogical manual)
primary_sources.role: Navya-Nyāya technical vocabulary, pratibandha doctrine, avacchedaka-avacchedya relations

primary_sources.full_name: Nyāya Sūtras of Gautama with Vātsyāyana Bhāṣya
primary_sources.author: Gautama (Gotama); commentary by Vātsyāyana
primary_sources.role: Original five-fold hetvābhāsa classification; foundational definitions

primary_sources.author: Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya

parent_categories.definition: A reason that is not uniformly concomitant with the conclusion — it deviates from the required pervasion in one of three possible ways
A reason that is pervaded by the negation of the conclusion — it proves the opposite of what is intended
A reason that is opposed by an equally strong reason proving the negation of the conclusion, leaving the matter inconclusive
A reason whose validity is not established — either its locus, its inherence in the subject, or its pervasion with the conclusion is unproved
A reason whose conclusion is overridden by a stronger, independent source of knowledge such as perception or established fact

extended_categories_note: RF-09 (Anyathāsiddha), RF-10 (Performative Self-Refutation), and RF-11 (Pratibandha) extend beyond the classical five-fold hetvābhāsa division. RF-09 derives from the causation theory in TS Sect. XXVI and NNB. RF-10 is an inferred category with no direct sūtra source. RF-11 derives from the pratibandha doctrine in NNB pp. 108–127. These extensions are clearly marked below.

categories.source_quote_english: The over-wide mark is that which is found both on the sapakṣa and the vipakṣa, that is, which co-exists both with the sādhya and its negation.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LIII, Nyāya-Bodhinī commentary: 'The sādhāraṇa or over-wide mark is that which is found both on the sapakṣa and the vipakṣa, that is, which co-exists both with sādhya and its negation.' Index entry: Sadharana- 44.
categories.definition_formal: Let H = reason-property, S = sādhya (conclusion-property). RF-01 holds when H is present in at least one instance where S is present (sapakṣa) AND H is present in at least one instance where S is absent (vipakṣa). The reason is underdetermined — it fails to discriminate between positive and negative cases.
categories.automation_notes: Requires domain knowledge to identify whether the reason-property appears in counter-instances. An LLM judge can assess whether the stated reason is too broad to establish the specific conclusion.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Is the reason-property restricted to cases where the conclusion holds, or does it also appear in cases where the conclusion does not hold?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka (limitor) on the reason is missing or too broad — it does not delimit the reason to the sādhya-relevant class.
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM provides a reason that is true but too generic to support the specific conclusion. The reason applies equally to cases where the conclusion holds and where it does not.

canonical_example_traditional.inference: The mountain has fire, because it is knowable (prameyatvāt)
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: Knowability (prameyatva) resides in the sapakṣa (kitchen with fire) AND in the vipakṣa (lake without fire). The reason is over-wide.

canonical_example_llm.inference: This drug should work because it has anti-inflammatory properties.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: Anti-inflammatory properties appear in drugs that DO work for this condition AND drugs that do NOT work for this condition (e.g., aspirin for viral infection). The reason fails to discriminate.
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: Restriction to the specific mechanism of action relevant to this pathology

categories.false_positive_notes: Risk of over-triggering on legitimately broad-but-valid reasons where the pervasion actually does hold universally. The scorer must check whether the reason genuinely appears in vipakṣa, not merely whether it could theoretically do so.
categories.distinguishing_features: Differs from RF-02 (asādhāraṇa) in that here the reason IS found on sapakṣa — the problem is excess, not deficiency. Differs from RF-03 (viruddha) in that the reason does not prove the opposite — it merely fails to prove anything determinate.

categories.source_quote_sanskrit: asādhāraṇo hetuḥ yaḥ pakṣa eva asti, na sapakṣa-vipakṣayoḥ
categories.source_quote_english: The asādhāraṇa or peculiar mark is that which is found neither in the sapakṣa nor in the vipakṣa — it is a peculiar characteristic of the pakṣa which exists nowhere else, and for which no sapakṣa can be found.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LIII, Nyāya-Bodhinī: 'The asādhāraṇa, in fact, as its name denotes, is a peculiar characteristic of the pakṣa which exists nowhere else, and for which therefore no sapakṣa can be found.' Index entry: Asadharana- 44, 299.
categories.definition_formal: Let H = reason-property, S = subject (pakṣa). RF-02 holds when H is found ONLY in S and not in any sapakṣa (positive instance) or vipakṣa (negative instance). A reason confined to a singleton cannot establish a general pervasion.
categories.automation_notes: Requires assessing whether the reason-property is unique to the subject. An LLM judge can flag when an argument's key premise relies on an idiosyncratic or non-generalizable property.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Is the reason-property found in any instance other than the specific subject? Can a general pervasion be established from it?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the reason is so narrow that it picks out only the pakṣa itself — no class can be formed, so no pervasion can be tested.
categories.llm_failure_type: Spurious causal reasoning from idiosyncratic property / non-generalizable reason
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM attributes a conclusion to a property unique to the subject, from which no general rule can be derived. Effectively, the argument is unfalsifiable because no comparison class exists.
categories.detection_rule: reason_present_only_in_subject(H, S) AND NOT reason_present_in_sapaksa(H) AND NOT reason_present_in_vipaksa(H)

canonical_example_traditional.inference: Sound is eternal, because it has the nature of sound (śabdatva)
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: Śabdatva (sound-nature) is a peculiar characteristic of sound alone. It exists in no sapakṣa (ether, etc.) and no vipakṣa (jar, etc.). No pervasion can be established.

canonical_example_llm.inference: Albert Einstein developed relativity because he was born in Ulm.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: Being born in Ulm is unique to Einstein among physicists who developed fundamental theories. No sapakṣa shares this property. No pervasion 'born in Ulm → develops revolutionary physics' can be established.
canonical_example_llm.failure_span: because he was born in Ulm
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: A generalizable property (e.g., mathematical training, creative thinking) that extends beyond the singleton

categories.false_positive_notes: This is a relatively clean detection — if the reason-property is genuinely unique to the subject, the fallacy is clear. Risk is mainly in edge cases where the property is rare but not truly unique.
categories.distinguishing_features: Opposite of RF-01: where RF-01 is over-wide, RF-02 is under-wide. Differs from RF-03 in that RF-02 does not prove the opposite — it simply proves nothing.

categories.source_quote_english: Contrary reason is that which is pervaded by the negation of the sādhya — the reason coincides with the opposite of the conclusion and not with the conclusion itself. The fallacy consists in drawing a conclusion just contrary to that which would be justified by the reason.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LIV: 'The viruddha or contrary reason is that which is less extensive than the negation of sādhya and never coexistent with sādhya.' Also: 'The fallacy consists in drawing a conclusion just contrary to that which would be justified by the reason. This accords well with Gotama's definition: a viruddha is that which is contrary to the conclusion desired to be drawn.' Gotama Sūtra I, 2, 47. Index: Viruddha- 44, 45, 206.
categories.definition_formal: Let H = reason-property, C = sādhya (conclusion). RF-03 holds when H is pervaded by NOT-C rather than C. That is: whenever H is present, NOT-C follows. The reason entails the opposite of the intended conclusion.
categories.automation_notes: Requires understanding the logical relationship between reason and conclusion to detect that the reason actually supports the opposite. This is often detectable by an LLM judge with domain knowledge.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Does the reason-property actually entail the conclusion, or does it entail the negation of the conclusion?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the vyāpti (pervasion) is inverted — the relation that actually holds is H → NOT-C, but the inference claims H → C.
categories.llm_failure_type: Self-contradictory reasoning / reason proves opposite of stated conclusion
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM provides a reason that, when examined logically, actually supports the opposite of the conclusion it draws. The direction of the inference is reversed.
categories.detection_rule: reason_pervades_negation(H, C) AND NOT reason_pervades_conclusion(H, C)

canonical_example_traditional.inference: Sound is eternal, because it is artificial (kṛtakatvāt)
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: Artificiality (kṛtakatva) is pervaded by non-eternality (anityatva), the opposite of eternality. The reason proves that sound is non-eternal, not eternal.

canonical_example_llm.inference: This policy is safe because it has never been tested.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: Never having been tested is pervaded by lack-of-established-safety, which is the negation of 'safe'. The reason proves the opposite of the stated conclusion.
canonical_example_llm.failure_span: because it has never been tested
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: The direction of the pervasion — 'untested' entails 'unestablished safety', not 'safety'

categories.false_positive_notes: When the contradiction is genuine, this is a high-confidence detection. Risk lies in cases where the relationship between reason and conclusion is ambiguous or context-dependent.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-01 (sādhāraṇa) in that RF-01 merely fails to prove the conclusion, while RF-03 actively proves the opposite. Distinguished from RF-08 (bādhita) in that RF-03's opposition comes from within the inference's own structure, while RF-08 involves an external defeating proof.

categories.source_quote_sanskrit: satpratipakṣo hetuḥ yatra sādhya-viparyayasya sādhanam api asti
categories.source_quote_english: The satpratipakṣa differs from viruddha in this: in viruddha the very same hetu proves the negation of the sādhya, whereas in satpratipakṣa the hetu proving the negation is different. An inference which is inconsequential owing to being counterbalanced by a contrary inference of equal weight does not remove the doubt.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LV: 'The satpratipakṣa differs from the viruddha in this, that while in the latter the very same hetu which ought to prove the sādhya is given as a reason for proving the sādhya-negation, in satpratipakṣa the hetu which proves sādhya-negation is different from that actually given.' Also: Gotama calls it 'prakaraṇasama' (inconclusive). Gotama Sūtra I, 2, 48. Index: Satpratipaksa- 44, 48, 84, 298.
categories.definition_formal: Let H1 = stated reason-property, C = conclusion, H2 = counter-reason-property. RF-04 holds when there exists a distinct H2 such that H2 establishes NOT-C with equal or greater strength than H1 establishes C, AND the inference fails to acknowledge or refute H2.
categories.automation_notes: CRITICAL LIMITATION: This is the one category that cannot be fully automated. Identifying whether an equally strong counter-reason exists requires domain expertise. In the scorer, RF-04 is flagged as 'requires human review' and must be labeled manually in the dataset. An LLM can suggest possible counter-reasons, but the strength comparison requires expert judgment.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Does an equally strong or stronger reason exist for the opposite conclusion, and has the inference acknowledged and addressed it?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the inference is incomplete — it has not delimited the domain of relevant evidence to exclude equally valid counter-evidence.
categories.llm_failure_type: Cherry-picking / one-sided reasoning / ignoring equally strong counter-evidence
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM presents a valid reason for a conclusion but ignores an equally valid reason for the opposite conclusion. The output appears confident but is actually inconclusive because the evidence is balanced.
categories.detection_rule: exists_counter_reason(H2, NOT_C) AND strength(H2, NOT_C) >= strength(H1, C) AND NOT acknowledges(inference, H2)

canonical_example_traditional.inference: Sound is eternal, because it is audible (like any other sound). Counter: Sound is non-eternal, because it is a creation (like a jar).
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: The reason 'audible' supports eternality; the counter-reason 'created' supports non-eternality with equal force. Neither prevails, and the inference is inconclusive.

canonical_example_llm.inference: Bitcoin is a good investment because it has delivered 100x returns over 10 years.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: Counter-reason: Bitcoin has experienced 80%+ drawdowns and has no intrinsic cash flow generating mechanism. Both reasons are valid; the inference cherry-picks one side.
canonical_example_llm.failure_span: because it has delivered 100x returns over 10 years
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: Acknowledgment and evaluation of equally strong counter-evidence (drawdown risk, volatility, lack of cash flow)

categories.false_positive_notes: Very high risk of both false positives (flagging valid one-sided arguments where the counter is actually weaker) and false negatives (missing counter-evidence that requires deep domain knowledge). This is why human review is mandatory.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-03 (viruddha) in that RF-03 involves the SAME reason proving the opposite, while RF-04 involves a DIFFERENT reason of equal strength. Distinguished from RF-08 (bādhita) in that RF-08 involves a stronger defeating proof, while RF-04 involves equal-weight opposition.

categories.source_quote_english: Non-existent subject: the skyey lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus like a lotus in a lake. Here skyey lotus is the subject, but it does not exist at all. Being misled by the metaphorical application of the word, we attribute the qualities of a real lotus to a fictitious thing.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LVI: 'Āśrayāsiddha is so called because in it the subject or place is devoid of the distinctive character of the supposed pakṣa. Thus in the example, A sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus — the pakṣa sky-lotus is only an imaginary thing, devoid of the essence of the supposed pakṣa.' Index: Asrayasiddha- 46. Also: Asiddha- 44, 46, 305.
categories.definition_formal: Let S = subject (pakṣa) of the inference. RF-05 holds when S does not exist — the entity referred to as the subject is fictitious, fabricated, or non-existent. All properties attributed to a non-existent locus are vacuously ungrounded.
categories.automation_notes: This is the most automatable category. Entity verification can be performed against knowledge bases, search engines, or structured databases. If the subject entity cannot be verified to exist, RF-05 fires.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Does the subject (pakṣa) of this inference actually exist?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka of the subject is empty — there is no real entity for the qualifier to delimit. The entire inference is grounded on a non-existent locus.
categories.llm_failure_type: Entity hallucination — fabricated subject (person, organization, study, event)
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM generates an inference about an entity that does not exist. The entity name may sound plausible but refers to no real person, organization, publication, or event.

canonical_example_traditional.inference: The sky-lotus (ākāśa-padma) is fragrant, because it is a lotus.
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: The sky-lotus does not exist. It is a fictitious entity. No properties can be validly inferred about it.

canonical_example_llm.inference: Dr. Sarah Chen's 2019 Stanford study shows that intermittent fasting reduces dementia risk by 47%.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: Dr. Sarah Chen does not exist. The study does not exist. The locus of the inference is entirely fabricated.

categories.false_positive_notes: Low when good entity verification is available. Risk increases for obscure but real entities that may not appear in standard knowledge bases. Also: newly created entities may not yet be indexed.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-06 (svarūpāsiddha) in that RF-05 involves a non-existent SUBJECT, while RF-06 involves a real subject with a non-existent PROPERTY. The TS commentary is explicit: 'In āśrayāsiddha the locus is either altogether non-existent or is not a proper pakṣa, while in svarūpāsiddha both pakṣa and āśraya may be real things but there is no connection between them.'

categories.source_quote_english: Non-existent reason: Sound is a quality because it is ocular. Here Sound is not ocular, as it is audible. The hetu itself is non-existent on the pakṣa — the reason-property does not actually reside in the subject.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LVI: 'The second variety, svarūpāsiddha, is so called because in it the hetu itself is asiddha, i.e. non-existent on the pakṣa. As in the example: Sound is a quality because it is ocular — the hetu (ocularity) does not exist on the pakṣa (sound).' Also: 'It differs from āśrayāsiddha in this, that in the latter the āśraya is either false or not a proper pakṣa, while in svarūpāsiddha both pakṣa and āśraya may be real things but there is no connection between them.' Index: Svarupasiddha- 46.
categories.definition_formal: Let S = subject (pakṣa), H = reason-property (hetu). RF-06 holds when S exists (real entity) BUT H does not actually inhere in S. The reason-property attributed to the subject is false.
categories.automation_notes: Property verification can be performed by checking claimed attributes against knowledge bases. If the subject exists but the attributed property is factually incorrect, RF-06 fires.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Does the reason-property (hetu) actually exist in the subject (pakṣa)?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka of the hetu is ungrounded in the pakṣa — the qualifier is placed on a real entity but the property it specifies does not actually reside there.
categories.llm_failure_type: Property hallucination — wrong attributes assigned to real entities
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM refers to a real entity but attributes a false property to it (wrong date, wrong characteristic, wrong achievement, wrong association).
categories.detection_rule: entity_exists(paksha) AND NOT property_verified(hetu, paksha, knowledge_base)

canonical_example_traditional.inference: Sound is a quality, because it is ocular (cākṣuṣatvāt).
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: Sound is a real entity (exists). But 'ocularity' (being perceived by the eye) does not reside in sound — sound is perceived by the ear, not the eye. The reason-property is non-existent in the subject.

canonical_example_llm.inference: The Eiffel Tower was built in 1820, therefore it pre-dates the Industrial Revolution.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: The Eiffel Tower exists (subject real). But 'built in 1820' is a false property — it was completed in 1889. The reason-property does not exist in the subject.
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: A verified, factually correct property attribution

categories.false_positive_notes: Low when good fact-checking is available. Risk increases for contested or nuanced properties where reasonable disagreement exists about what is 'correct'.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-05 in that the SUBJECT exists but the PROPERTY is false. Distinguished from RF-07a/b in that RF-06 is about the hetu's inherence in the pakṣa, while RF-07a/b is about the vyāpti (pervasion) between hetu and sādhya.

categories.english: Unestablished Pervasion — Missing Universal Qualifier (Upādhi Problem)
categories.source_text: TS Sect. LVI (final sub-section on vyāpyatvāsiddha); TS Sect. on Upādhi (§ 46–47)
categories.source_quote_sanskrit: vyāpyatvāsiddhe sopādhibhūto hetuḥ — upadhi-sahita-vyāptiḥ na nirūpādhikā
categories.source_quote_english: Non-existent concomitance is one which involves a limitation or condition (upādhi). Condition is that which pervades the thing to be proved but does not pervade the reason. In 'the mountain is smoky because it has fire', contact with wet fuel is the condition.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LVI: 'Non-existent concomitance is one which involves a limitation or condition. Condition is that which pervades the thing to be proved, but does not pervade the reason. Pervasion of the thing to be proved means not having absolute negation co-existent with the thing; while non-pervasion of reason means having absolute negation co-existing with the reason. In the mountain is smoky because it has fire, contact with wet fuel is the condition.' Index: Vyapyatvasiddha- 46; Upadhi- 46, 47, 310; Sopadhika- 46.
categories.definition_formal: Let H = reason, C = conclusion, U = upādhi (qualifier/condition). RF-07a holds when the stated pervasion H → C is actually conditional: (H ∧ U) → C. The upādhi U pervades the sādhya C but does not pervade the hetu H. The inference presents a conditional pervasion as if it were unconditional.
categories.automation_notes: Detecting missing qualifiers requires domain knowledge about the conditions under which a pervasion holds. An LLM judge can identify common upādhis in well-known domains (medicine, law, engineering). Less automatable in novel domains.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Is the stated pervasion (vyāpti) between reason and conclusion unconditional, or does it require an additional qualifier (upādhi) that is not stated?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the vyāpti is missing — the pervasion is conditional (sopādhika) but presented as unconditional (nirupādhika). The upādhi must be identified and checked for presence.
categories.llm_failure_type: Missing qualifiers / unconditional claim where conditions apply
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM states a general rule as unconditionally true when it actually depends on conditions not mentioned. The inference works only when certain additional qualifiers are present, but these are omitted.

canonical_example_traditional.inference: The mountain is smoky, because it has fire.
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: Fire does not universally produce smoke. Contact with wet fuel (ārdrā-indhana-saṃyoga) is the upādhi — smoke arises only when fire contacts wet fuel. The pervasion 'fire → smoke' is conditional, not universal.

canonical_example_llm.analysis: The pervasion 'antibiotics → cures infection' is conditional on: (1) bacterial type, (2) antibiotic resistance status, (3) correct dosing, (4) patient not having contraindications. The LLM presents the pervasion as unconditional.
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: Bacterial type qualifier, resistance status qualifier, dosing qualifier, contraindication check

categories.false_positive_notes: Risk of over-triggering by demanding qualifiers for pervasions that are genuinely universal or near-universal in the relevant context. The scorer must assess whether the missing qualifier is materially relevant, not merely theoretically possible.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-07b in scope: RF-07a is about the GENERAL pervasion being conditional (the rule itself needs a qualifier), while RF-07b is about the pervasion failing for THIS SPECIFIC subject even though the general rule holds. Distinguished from RF-06 in that RF-06 is about the hetu's inherence in the pakṣa, while RF-07a is about the vyāpti between hetu and sādhya.

categories.english: Unestablished Pervasion — Missing Contextual Qualifier for This Subject
categories.source_text: TS Sect. LVI (commentary elaboration); NNB pp. 60–72
categories.source_quote_sanskrit: Elaboration in TS commentary on upadhi sub-types and NNB treatment of avacchedaka-specific pervasion failure
categories.source_quote_english: The upadhi may be present in the general case but absent in the specific pakṣa. When the qualifier required for the pervasion to hold in this specific subject is absent, the pervasion is unestablished for this particular inference even though it may hold generally.
categories.source_verification: This is derived from the TS commentary's discussion of upādhi varieties and the NNB's treatment of how avacchedaka-specific conditions can defeat a pervasion that is generally valid. The TS commentary at Sect. LVI discusses multiple sub-varieties of asiddha including cases where 'the negation of the hetu, and not the hetu, resides in the pakṣa.' The NNB pp. 60–72 treats contextual pervasion failure through avacchedaka analysis.
categories.confidence_basis: VERIFIED for the underlying concept; the specific RF-07b coding as a distinct sub-type from RF-07a is an INFERRED structural decision for product purposes
categories.definition_formal: Let H = reason, C = conclusion, S = specific subject, U_s = subject-specific qualifier. RF-07b holds when the general pervasion H → C is established, BUT there exists a specific condition of this particular subject S such that the pervasion does not hold for S. The upādhi is contextual to the individual case.
categories.automation_notes: Requires knowledge of the specific subject's attributes to determine if contextual conditions defeat the general pervasion. More domain-specific than RF-07a. An LLM judge with access to context about the subject can assess this.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Even if the general pervasion holds, does it hold for THIS specific subject given its particular attributes and context?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the pakṣa reveals a contextual condition that defeats the general vyāpti for this particular case. The general rule is valid but does not apply here.
categories.llm_failure_type: Failure to apply relevant context / ignoring subject-specific exceptions
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM applies a general rule to a specific case where subject-specific conditions make the rule inapplicable. The general principle is correct, but not for this particular instance.
categories.detection_rule: general_vyapti_established(H, C) AND subject_has_defeating_condition(S, context) AND condition_not_acknowledged(inference_text)

canonical_example_traditional.inference: This son of Mitrā is dark-coloured, because he is a son of Mitrā, like his elder brothers.
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: The elder brothers' dark colour came from their mother eating only vegetables. But this particular son was born after she ate ghee. The general association (son of Mitrā → dark) does not hold for this specific pakṣa because the contextual condition (vegetable diet) is absent.

canonical_example_llm.inference: This patient should take ibuprofen because ibuprofen reduces fever.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: The general pervasion 'ibuprofen → reduces fever' is established. But this specific patient has kidney disease. The contextual qualifier 'no renal impairment' is absent for this subject. The general rule does not apply here.
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: Subject-specific qualifier: no renal impairment, no NSAID contraindication for this patient

categories.false_positive_notes: Risk of over-triggering by flagging theoretically possible but practically irrelevant contextual exceptions. The scorer must assess the materiality of the defeating condition, not merely its theoretical possibility.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-07a in that RF-07a is about the GENERAL rule being conditional, while RF-07b is about the general rule being valid but inapplicable to THIS SPECIFIC case. Distinguished from RF-06 in that the hetu DOES reside in the pakṣa — the problem is in the vyāpti, not the hetu's inherence.

categories.english: Defeated Reason — Contradicted by Stronger Evidence
categories.source_quote_sanskrit: bādhito hetuḥ yatra sādhyam anya-pramāṇena nivāryate
categories.source_quote_english: A reason is false (bādhita) where the negation of the thing to be proved is established by another proof. The special characteristic of bādhita is that the sādhya is disproved by another and presumably more authoritative proof; for if the other proof is not stronger, it will not prevail.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LVII: 'The special characteristic of bādhita has been already explained in distinguishing it from satpratipakṣa. Annambhaṭṭa defines it as a hetu designed to prove a sādhya, the negation of which is ascertained by another and presumably a more authoritative proof.' Also: 'In bādhita the sādhya of the inference in question is actually disproved by a stronger proof of another kind, such as perception.' Gotama Sūtra reference. Index: Badhita- 44, 48, 315.
categories.definition_formal: Let H = reason, C = conclusion, K = independent knowledge source (perception, established fact, stronger inference). RF-08 holds when K directly establishes NOT-C, thereby defeating the conclusion C generated by H. The defeating evidence is external to the inference's own structure.
categories.automation_notes: For factual claims, this can be automated by checking the conclusion against verified fact databases. For more complex claims, an LLM judge can assess whether established knowledge contradicts the conclusion. The key distinguishing factor from RF-04 is that RF-08 involves a STRONGER defeating proof, not an equally balanced counter-reason.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Is the conclusion contradicted by a known fact, established perception, or stronger proof from an independent source?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the sādhya is overridden — the conclusion has a qualifier that conflicts with independently established knowledge. The inference's internal logic may be sound, but the conclusion is externally defeated.
categories.llm_failure_type: Contradicting known facts / conclusion disproved by verifiable information
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM produces an inference that is internally structured but whose conclusion contradicts well-established, independently verifiable facts.

canonical_example_traditional.inference: Fire is cold, because it is a substance.
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: The inference has internal structure. But the conclusion 'fire is cold' is directly defeated by tactile perception (sparśa-pratyakṣa) — we perceive fire as hot. The bādhaka-pramāṇa (defeating proof) is perception.

canonical_example_llm.inference: The Earth must be the center of the solar system because the Sun appears to move across the sky.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: The inference has formal structure. But the conclusion is defeated by established heliocentric astronomical evidence (bādhaka pramāṇa). The defeating proof is overwhelmingly stronger.
canonical_example_llm.failure_span: The Earth must be the center of the solar system
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: Acknowledgment of independently established astronomical evidence that defeats this conclusion

categories.false_positive_notes: Low for factual claims where the defeating evidence is clear and well-established. Risk increases for conclusions in contested domains where what counts as 'established fact' is itself debated.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-03 (viruddha) in that RF-03's opposition comes from WITHIN the inference (the reason itself proves the opposite), while RF-08's opposition comes from OUTSIDE (an independent proof defeats the conclusion). Distinguished from RF-04 (satpratipakṣa) in that RF-04 involves equal-strength opposition, while RF-08 involves a clearly stronger defeating proof.

categories.english: Explained by Another Cause — Causally Redundant Reason
categories.source_text: TS Sect. XXVI (causation theory); NNB pp. 87–93
categories.source_quote_sanskrit: anyathāsiddho hetuḥ yasya kāryatva-ādi-sambandho anyena eva siddhaḥ
categories.source_quote_english: Anyathāsiddha: that which is 'otherwise established' — the causal relation is already accounted for by another independent cause. From the TS causation discussion: 'ananyathāsiddha' (not-otherwise-established) is a required condition for valid causation, meaning the cause must not be causally redundant.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. XXVI and commentary extensively discuss anyathāsiddha in the context of causation theory. The NNB p. 87 discusses anyathāsiddha as a concept: 'anyathā anyaprakāreṇa kāryasya kṛṣṇakāraṇa-bhinnatva-rūpeṇa siddhāḥ prasiddhā'. Index entry: Anyathasiddha- 26, 192. NOTE: Anyathāsiddha is primarily a CAUSAL concept in the original texts, not a named hetvābhāsa. Its classification as a distinct reasoning failure mode (RF-09) is an INFERRED extension for product purposes.
categories.confidence_basis: VERIFIED for the concept and its textual source; INFERRED for its classification as a distinct hetvābhāsa category (the texts treat anyathāsiddha as a causal concept, not as one of the five named fallacies)
categories.definition_formal: Let H = proposed reason/cause, C = conclusion/effect, K = independent alternative cause. RF-09 holds when K already fully accounts for the observed effect C, making H causally redundant. H may be present and real, but its causal role is unnecessary.
categories.automation_notes: Requires domain knowledge to assess whether an alternative explanation fully accounts for the observed phenomenon. An LLM judge with relevant domain training can identify common cases of spurious causation.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Is the proposed reason (hetu) actually causally necessary for the conclusion, or is the conclusion already fully explained by an independent cause?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the kāraṇatā (causation) is redundant — the causal relation claimed between reason and conclusion is 'otherwise established' by an independent mechanism.
categories.llm_failure_type: Spurious causal attribution / post hoc ergo propter hoc / ignoring confounders
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM attributes a conclusion to a cause that is causally redundant — the effect is already fully explained by an independent cause. The proposed reason is real and present but not causally necessary.
categories.detection_rule: exists_independent_cause(K, C, context) AND K_fully_explains(C) AND H_is_redundant(H, K, C)

canonical_example_traditional.inference: The potter's ass is the cause of the pot, because it carries the clay that is used to make the pot.
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: The clay can be brought by hand or cart. The ass is an antecedent but not an invariable (niyata) antecedent. The pot is explained by the potter's skill and materials, not by the particular transport mechanism.
canonical_example_traditional.source: TS Sect. XXVI (causation discussion — the potter's ass example)

canonical_example_llm.inference: The patient recovered because we administered homeopathic remedy X.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: The recovery is fully explained by the immune system's natural response over the same time period. The proposed cause (remedy X) is causally redundant — the effect is 'anyathāsiddha' (otherwise established).
canonical_example_llm.failure_span: because we administered homeopathic remedy X
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: Evidence of causal necessity — that the effect would NOT have occurred without the proposed cause

categories.false_positive_notes: High risk because determining causal necessity vs. redundancy is inherently difficult. Multiple causes may genuinely contribute (overdetermination). The scorer should flag, not definitively classify, unless the alternative explanation is clearly sufficient.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-01 (sādhāraṇa) in that RF-01 is about the reason being too broad, while RF-09 is about the reason being causally unnecessary. Distinguished from RF-08 (bādhita) in that RF-08 defeats the CONCLUSION, while RF-09 defeats the CAUSAL LINK between reason and conclusion.

categories.source_quote_sanskrit: N/A — This is an inferred category
categories.source_quote_english: N/A — This category is constructed from the intersection of viruddha (RF-03) and bādhita (RF-08). The act of asserting the claim provides the defeating evidence (bādhita), and the reason given proves the opposite of the conclusion (viruddha).
categories.source_verification: CRITICAL NOTE: This category has NO direct sūtra or commentary source in any of the four texts in the project corpus. It is a structural inference from the combination of RF-03 (viruddha — the reason proves the opposite) and RF-08 (bādhita — the conclusion is defeated by another proof). The 'other proof' in this case is the performative act of assertion itself. This derivation is defensible but must be explicitly stated as INFERRED in the arXiv paper.
categories.confidence_basis: INFERRED — No direct textual source. Constructed from viruddha + bādhita intersection. Defensible as a special case but not a named category in the tradition.
categories.definition_formal: Let A = the act of asserting the claim, C = the content of the claim. RF-10 holds when A itself constitutes evidence that defeats C. The performative conditions of the assertion contradict the propositional content of the assertion.
categories.automation_notes: Detectable by checking whether the claim's truth-conditions are undermined by the act of making the claim. An LLM judge can identify common forms of performative contradiction.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Does the act of asserting this claim undermine the very conditions under which the claim could be true?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka of the assertion includes the negation of the assertion itself — the claim is self-defeating because its performative conditions contradict its content.
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM produces a claim that is undermined by the very act of producing it. The output's existence contradicts the output's content.

canonical_example_traditional.inference: N/A — No traditional Nyāya example exists for this category
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: This is an inferred category. The closest structural analogue in the tradition would be a viruddha where the hetu is the act of speaking itself.

canonical_example_llm.inference: I am completely certain that no claims can be made with certainty.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: The act of claiming certainty (performative condition) contradicts the content of the claim (no certainty is possible). The assertion self-refutes.
canonical_example_llm.failure_span: I am completely certain that no claims can be made with certainty
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: Consistency between the performative conditions of the assertion and its propositional content

categories.false_positive_notes: Low when the self-refutation is clear. Risk increases in cases where the apparent self-refutation depends on equivocation between different senses of a term.
categories.distinguishing_features: Unique in that the defeating evidence is the ASSERTION ITSELF, not an external fact (RF-08) or the internal logic of the reason (RF-03). This is the only category with no direct textual source — it must be flagged as INFERRED in all documentation.

categories.source_quote_sanskrit: pratibandhakatvam — pratibadhyati bādhate yaḥ sa pratibandhakaḥ, tasya bhāvaḥ pratibandhakatvam. tac ca kāraṇībhūtābhāva-pratiyogitvam, kāryānutpāda-prayojakatvam
categories.source_quote_english: Blockerhood: that which blocks or restrains is a pratibandha (blocker); its nature is blockerhood (pratibandhakatva). It is: (1) being the counter-positive of an absence that is a cause, (2) being the promoter of non-production of the effect. When all causal conditions are present but a blocking entity exists, the effect does not arise.
categories.source_verification: NNB pp. 72–80: 'pratibandhakatvam — pratibadhyati bādhate yaḥ sa pratibandhakaḥ, tasya bhāvaḥ pratibandhakatvam. tac ca kāraṇībhūtābhāva-pratiyogitvam, kāryānutpāda-prayojakatvam.' The NNB then gives the jewel-fire example (maṇi): a specific jewel placed near fire blocks the burning even though all causal conditions for burning are present. Also: 'there exists a particular kind of jewel which, when present near fire, blocks the burning — its absence is the condition required for the causal chain to complete.' VERIFIED for the concept. INFERRED for hetvābhāsa classification.
categories.confidence_basis: VERIFIED for the concept of pratibandha and its textual source in NNB. INFERRED for its classification as a reasoning failure mode — the texts treat pratibandha as a causal-epistemological concept, not as a named hetvābhāsa.
categories.definition_formal: Let H = reason/causal conditions, C = conclusion/effect, B = blocking condition (pratibandha). RF-11 holds when all standard causal conditions for C are present, BUT a blocking condition B is also present which prevents the causal chain from completing. The inference would be valid if B were absent, but B's presence defeats it.
categories.automation_notes: Requires domain-specific knowledge of blocking conditions. In medicine: drug interactions, genetic variants. In law: exceptions, safe harbors. An LLM judge with domain knowledge can identify common blockers.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Are all causal conditions present for the conclusion, AND is there an unacknowledged blocking condition that prevents the causal chain from completing?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the kāraṇatā (causal chain) is blocked — there exists a pratibandha whose absence is required for the effect to occur, but the inference does not acknowledge this blocker.
categories.llm_failure_type: Ignoring blocking conditions / unacknowledged inhibitors / drug interactions / exception conditions
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM presents all causal conditions as sufficient but fails to account for a blocking condition that prevents the expected outcome. The causal chain is structurally complete but practically blocked.
categories.detection_rule: all_causal_conditions_present(H, C) AND exists_blocker(B, C, context) AND blocker_not_acknowledged(B, inference_text)

canonical_example_traditional.inference: Fire will burn this object, because fire is present and the object is combustible.
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: All causal conditions are present. But a specific jewel (maṇi) is placed near the fire, which blocks the burning. The jewel is the pratibandha. Its absence is the condition required for the causal chain to complete.

canonical_example_llm.inference: This medication will eliminate the tumor — it has proven efficacy against this cancer type.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: All standard causal conditions are present (correct drug, correct cancer type, correct dosage). But the patient has MDR1 gene overexpression, which blocks drug absorption at the cellular level. The causal chain is structurally complete but blocked.
canonical_example_llm.failure_span: This medication will eliminate the tumor
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: Subject-specific blocking condition: MDR1 overexpression preventing drug absorption

categories.false_positive_notes: Risk of over-triggering by identifying theoretically possible blockers that are not actually present or relevant. The scorer must verify that the blocking condition is actually active in the specific case, not merely possible in theory.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-07b in that RF-07b is about a missing qualifier on the PERVASION (the rule doesn't apply), while RF-11 is about a BLOCKER on the CAUSAL CHAIN (the rule applies but an inhibitor is present). Distinguished from RF-08 (bādhita) in that RF-08 defeats the conclusion with external evidence, while RF-11 accepts the causal structure but identifies an internal blockage.

categories.source_quote_sanskrit: anupasamhārī hetuḥ yatra sādhyam eva viśvavyāpi
categories.source_quote_english: The anupasamhārī or non-exclusive reason is one where the sādhya being universal, nothing is excluded from it. The name 'non-exclusive' is given to this fallacy because the sādhya being universal nothing is excluded from it.
categories.source_verification: TS Sect. LIII: 'The proper answer to the first objection would be that in an anupasamhārī, although there may be individual things in which the hetu is ascertained, there is no sapakṣa either of the sādhāraṇa or of the asādhāraṇa kind, since the conclusion itself constitutes the widest possible generalization. The name Non-Exclusive is given to this fallacy because the sādhya being universal nothing is excluded from it.' Index: Anupasarhhāri- 44, 302.
categories.definition_formal: Let H = reason-property, C = conclusion. RF-12 holds when C is so universal that it applies to everything — no vipakṣa (counter-instance) exists, and therefore no meaningful pervasion between H and C can be tested. The conclusion is trivially true or unfalsifiable.
categories.automation_notes: Detectable by checking whether the conclusion admits any counter-instance at all. If the sādhya is universally true, the inference is vacuous — it proves nothing non-trivial.
categories.avacchedaka_question: Does the conclusion admit any counter-instance (vipakṣa), or is it so universal that it cannot be meaningfully tested?
categories.avacchedaka_diagnosis: The avacchedaka on the sādhya has no boundary — the conclusion is so broad that it cannot be delimited, and therefore the pervasion between hetu and sādhya cannot be meaningfully established.
categories.llm_failure_type: Vacuous / unfalsifiable conclusion / trivially universal claim
categories.llm_failure_description: The LLM produces a conclusion so broad or universal that it is unfalsifiable — it applies to everything and therefore proves nothing specific. The inference may be formally structured but is informationally vacuous.

canonical_example_traditional.inference: All things are nameable, because they are knowable.
canonical_example_traditional.analysis: The sādhya 'nameable' is universal — everything is nameable. There is no vipakṣa (nothing is not-nameable). Since nothing can be excluded, the pervasion cannot be tested and the inference is vacuous.

canonical_example_llm.inference: AI systems have properties, because they are computational entities.
canonical_example_llm.analysis: The conclusion 'has properties' is universally true of all entities. No counter-instance exists. The inference is trivially true and proves nothing meaningful.
canonical_example_llm.missing_avacchedaka: A non-trivial, falsifiable conclusion that admits counter-instances

categories.false_positive_notes: Low because truly vacuous/universal conclusions are relatively easy to identify. Risk is mainly in edge cases where the conclusion appears specific but is actually unfalsifiable under examination.
categories.distinguishing_features: Distinguished from RF-01 (sādhāraṇa) in that RF-01 is about the REASON being too broad, while RF-12 is about the CONCLUSION being too broad. Distinguished from RF-02 (asādhāraṇa) in that RF-02 has no sapakṣa (too narrow), while RF-12 has no vipakṣa (too wide). Together, the three savyabhicāra sub-types exhaust the possible ways the reason can fail to properly track the conclusion.

avacchedaka_operator.definition: That which 'cuts off' — a property or relation that determines the exact scope within which a given logical relation holds. The term has at least three meanings: distinguishing (viśeṣaṇa), particularizing (ekadeśa), and determining (niyāmaka).
avacchedaka_operator.source_text: TS Appendix H (Cowell's Note on Kusumāñjali of Udayanācārya)
avacchedaka_operator.source_quote: The term Avacehedaka has at least three meanings: as distinguishing, particularizing and determining. Wherever we find a relation which is not itself included in any one of the seven categories but is common to several, we require something to determine its different varieties. Thus if we say that fire is the cause of smoke, we require, to determine this particular relation of causality, something which shall be always found present with it. Thus in 'fire is the cause of smoke' it will be vahnitva, the species of all fires.
avacchedaka_operator.source_verification: TS Appendix H, verbatim from the edition in the project corpus. This is the foundational passage for the avacchedaka concept as used in this project.
avacchedaka_operator.role_in_taxonomy: Master diagnostic operator. Every RF category is ultimately an avacchedaka failure — a failure of the proper qualifier on the subject (pakṣa), the reason (hetu), the pervasion (vyāpti), or the causal chain. The avacchedaka-question field in each category specifies the exact form this failure takes.

distinguishing.example: In 'a blue lotus', 'blue' is the distinguishing avacchedaka of the lotus — it distinguishes it from others of different colours.

particularizing.example: In 'the bird sits on the tree on the branch', 'branch' particularizes the exact spot — this is the ekadeśa-avacchedaka.

determining.example: In 'fire is the cause of smoke', vahnitva (fire-ness) determines this particular causal relation — it is the dhūma-kāraṇatā-avacchedaka.

per_category_mapping.RF-01: Missing restriction on the reason — the avacchedaka of the hetu does not delimit it to the sādhya-relevant class
per_category_mapping.RF-02: Overly narrow reason — the avacchedaka of the hetu picks out only the pakṣa, preventing pervasion
per_category_mapping.RF-03: Inverted pervasion — the avacchedaka on the vyāpti maps H to NOT-C instead of C
per_category_mapping.RF-04: Incomplete evidence delimitation — the avacchedaka on the inference scope fails to include counter-evidence
per_category_mapping.RF-05: Empty subject — the avacchedaka of the pakṣa refers to a non-existent entity
per_category_mapping.RF-06: False property — the avacchedaka of the hetu attributes a non-existent property to the pakṣa
per_category_mapping.RF-07a: Missing universal qualifier — the avacchedaka on the vyāpti omits the upādhi required for the pervasion
per_category_mapping.RF-07b: Missing contextual qualifier — the avacchedaka on the pakṣa-specific vyāpti omits the subject-specific condition
per_category_mapping.RF-08: Externally defeated conclusion — the avacchedaka on the sādhya conflicts with independently established knowledge
per_category_mapping.RF-09: Causally redundant reason — the avacchedaka on the kāraṇatā is 'otherwise established' by an independent cause
per_category_mapping.RF-10: Self-defeating assertion — the avacchedaka of the assertion includes the negation of the assertion itself
per_category_mapping.RF-11: Blocked causal chain — the avacchedaka on the kāraṇatā is blocked by a pratibandha whose absence is required
per_category_mapping.RF-12: Universal conclusion — the avacchedaka on the sādhya has no boundary and admits no vipakṣa

inferred_notes.RF-09: Concept verified in TS Sect. XXVI and NNB. Classification as distinct hetvābhāsa is inferred — the texts treat anyathāsiddha as a causal concept, not a named fallacy.
inferred_notes.RF-10: No direct sūtra source. Constructed from viruddha (RF-03) + bādhita (RF-08) intersection. Must be explicitly flagged in arXiv paper.
inferred_notes.RF-11: Concept verified in NNB pp. 72–80. Classification as distinct hetvābhāsa is inferred — the texts treat pratibandha as an epistemological concept, not a named fallacy.

known_gaps: RF-04 (Satpratipakṣa) cannot be fully automated — requires human review for counter-reason identification and strength comparison.

RF-07b's status as a sub-type distinct from RF-07a is a product-level structural decision, not a distinction explicitly drawn in the source texts. The texts discuss upādhi varieties but do not name RF-07b as a separate category.
RF-09, RF-10, and RF-11 extend beyond the classical five-fold hetvābhāsa classification. This must be transparent in all documentation.

The OCR quality of the Tarka-Saṃgraha text in the project corpus is imperfect — some Sanskrit passages are garbled. Source quotes should be verified against a clean critical edition before arXiv submission.
The Tattva-Cintāmaṇi text in the corpus has significant OCR issues and could not be used for direct verification of advanced vyāpti formulations.
